newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INSTANT VIEW - Australian retail trade data.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Australian retail trade data.

text.p: Australian retail trade fell 0.3 percent in March, official figures showed on Friday.
In the March quarter, real retail trade rose 2.2 percent, the data showed.
Economists' median forecasts had centred on a flat monthly result and a 2.4 percent rise in real terms in the March quarter.
A selection of economists immediate reactions to the data follow.
AKIS HARALABOPOULOS, SENIOR ECONOMIST, GIO AUSTRALIA

"No reason for concern even though there is a modest fall of 0.3 percent. The important thing to focus on in the retail trade figures is the quarterly numbers showing a 2.2 percent increase in the quarter, and if you plug that into your spreadsheet for the March quarter national accounts, we're looking for an increase in GDP (A) of around 1.0 percent, that's our ballpark figure. The quarterly number is encouraging, your monthly numbers are disappointing, but when it's all said and done, the bottom line is it's not going to change the way our policy makers are thinking on official interest rates."
SHANE OLIVER, CHIEF ECONOMIST, AMP INVESTMENTS:

"You have seen strong growth through the quarter, but there is some argument that a lot of that was just a rebound from a very weak December quarter and to that extent, seasonal problems may have been involved. But I would think the soft number in March wouldn't really change the Reserve Bank's view of things and for the time being they would probably be inclined to sit back, at least for the next month."
STEPHEN KOUKOULAS, CHIEF ECONOMIST CITIBANK AUSTRALIA:

"The worst is behind the retail sector in that it's stopped declining. The early stages of some sort of pick-up are eventuating, despite the monthly decline. It's not a boom, but with the lift in incomes we are seeing and also the cuts in mortgage rates still to filter through to people's hip pocket, there is probably more upside to the retail sector for the remainder of the year. The early stages of a recovery are starting to emerge."
DAVID LANSLEY, TREASURY ECONOMIST, NATIONAL AUSTRALIA BANK:

"(On if it would lead to market talk of rate cuts) I don't think they're going to be looking to an easing. I think the key thing really still is wages in terms of what the (Reserve) Bank is looking at. The only way I'd see an easing coming from consumer spending is if we get a run of very weak numbers. I don't think one monthly number is going to feed much into the Reserve Bank's calculations at all, and they'll be happy just to sit back, a little bit nervous about the outlook for wages in the medium term perhaps, and leave rates where they are."
HANS KUNNEN, GROUP ECONOMIST, COLONIAL STATE BANK:

"The pullback really had to come, but the March quarter growth is still firm. It doesn't really add either way to rate cut speculation for or against. To raise rate cut speculation the fall had to be harder than that. It wasn't an especially big pullback, the Reserve Bank is still going to be on hold."
STEPHEN ROBERTS, CHIEF ECONOMIST AT UBS AUSTRALIA:

"It suggests that the bit of a pick which we saw in retail activity in January and February has faded back somewhat in March. It just reconfirms that the data is very patchy at the moment. Sure it's going to make a positive contribution to GDP growth in the March quarter...but the way it is look now GDP is still going to be languishing at 3.0-ish percent. If it wasn't for that average weekly earnings number yesterday, we would still be agonising whether they would be a rate cut or not. All the other data we have seen so far has been on the somewhat sluggish side."
